items.title: From Fair Representation to Just Recognition in Generative AI
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.12669v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The fair AI/ML literature has long distinguished distributive fairness, concerning how automated systems allocate resources and opportunities, from representational fairness, concerning how they shape the ways individuals and social groups are perceived, understood, and accorded social status. Generative AI is rebalancing these normative dimensions. Unlike predictive systems, large language models (LLMs) and related technologies are fundamentally expressive: their primary function is to convey meaning rather than automate domain-specific decisions. Representational harm has also become central to value alignment, especially in research on what and whose values and perspectives AI systems should represent. Existing approaches to harms in the representation of social groups often appeal to descriptive accuracy, but this strategy has important limitations. For many social groups, no stable or bounded referent exists against which representational accuracy can be judged. It is also unclear who has the authority to decide what counts as misrepresentation, while even accurate representations can reproduce harmful social patterns. The underlying problem, we argue, is therefore not simply misrepresentation but misrecognition. Drawing on political theory, especially Nancy Fraser's account of participatory parity, we show how moving from representational fairness to recognitional justice provides better conceptual and normative tools for governing central fairness challenges in generative AI.
items.claude_summary: When generative AI systems misrepresent social groups, the problem is not simply that they get facts wrong — it is that they deny those groups the social standing to define themselves. This paper argues that existing 'representational fairness' frameworks, which measure AI outputs against some presumed accurate description of a group, are conceptually inadequate: many groups have no stable, agreed-upon referent against which accuracy can be judged, authority over what counts as misrepresentation is contested, and even accurate depictions can perpetuate harmful social hierarchies. Drawing on political theorist Nancy Fraser's concept of participatory parity, the authors propose replacing representational fairness with 'recognitional justice' — a framework that asks not whether AI outputs are accurate but whether they afford all social groups equal standing to participate in public life.
items.centre_angle: This paper argues that fairness in generative AI cannot be reduced to descriptive accuracy — the real normative question is whether AI systems afford social groups equal standing to participate in defining themselves. From CAMO's perspective on trustworthy AI-driven decisions, the implication is that evaluation frameworks which treat fairness as a measurement problem may systematically miss a class of harms that are relational and political rather than statistical. Organizations deploying large language models for communication, content generation, or customer-facing applications face governance questions that their existing data-quality and bias-audit toolkits are not designed to answer.
items.key_takeaway: Auditing generative AI for representational fairness requires political and normative frameworks, not just accuracy benchmarks — a distinction that has direct consequences for how organizations govern LLM deployments.

items.title: AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency in Hybrid Human-AI Cognition
items.authors: Jochen Kuhn, Peter Gerjets, Ulrich Trautwein, Jeffrey A. Greene, Sarah Malone, Patrik Vogt, Tim F\"utterer
items.summary:
arXiv:2608.21618v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (genAI) systems are increasingly integral to epistemic processes such as hypothesis generation, explanation construction, and decision-making. Although they reliably enhance performance, emerging evidence reveals a metacognitive dilemma: as external generative capacity increases, internal monitoring, calibration, and cognitive engagement may decline. This reflects a redistribution of cognitive control within distributed human-AI systems that cannot be explained by automation bias or reliance on algorithms alone. We propose the AIRIS (AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems) framework to analyze this dilemma and specify where regulatory intervention can counteract it. AIRIS is a multi-level control allocation architecture specifying the conditions under which epistemic agency can be preserved in hybrid generative systems. Drawing on distributed cognition, cognitive load theory, multimedia learning, and self-regulated learning, it identifies seven interacting mechanisms through which hybrid cognition may become destabilized, from delegation and calibration drift to motivational-affective drift. Five regulatory operators (Anticipate, Interrogate, Reflect, Integrate, and Synthesize) target internal generative engagement at points of emerging instability. The architecture does not itself improve learning; it specifies what must remain in place for genAI-supported work to sustain understanding, whether through instructional design, teacher guidance, or learners' own regulation. We derive testable propositions concerning the seven mechanisms and the five operators, reframing AI augmentation as a problem of control allocation in distributed generative systems. Beyond theory, AIRIS offers a research agenda, a design framework for genAI-integrated learning environments, and a conceptual toolkit for the governance of hybrid human-AI cognition.
items.claude_summary: When generative AI handles more of the cognitive heavy lifting, humans may quietly stop doing the internal work that produces genuine understanding. This paper introduces AIRIS, a multi-level framework diagnosing seven ways hybrid human-AI cognition can become destabilized — including delegation drift, calibration drift, and motivational-affective drift — and proposes five regulatory operators to keep human epistemic agency intact. The framework draws on distributed cognition and self-regulated learning theory, and is aimed at instructional designers, educators, and governance bodies. Crucially, AIRIS does not itself improve learning or performance; it specifies the structural conditions that must be preserved for AI-assisted work to sustain real understanding rather than surface-level output.
items.centre_angle: This paper argues that as generative AI absorbs more of the cognitive process, it can erode the internal monitoring and sustained engagement that produce genuine competence — a risk that applies well beyond classrooms. From CAMO's perspective on AI and incentives, this resonates directly with findings in 'Better Technology, Worse Motivation: GenAI and the Mediocrity Trap,' where AI assistance was shown to flatten the quality curve and reduce professionals' motivation to sustain effort toward excellence. The AIRIS framework adds theoretical architecture to that empirical observation: the issue is not automation bias alone, but a systematic redistribution of cognitive control that may require deliberate structural countermeasures at the organizational and governance level.

matched_camo.reason: Both works identify a paradox in which AI assistance reduces the internal effort and sustained engagement required for high-quality output, with AIRIS providing theoretical mechanisms and CAMO's paper providing experimental evidence in a professional creative context.

items.key_takeaway: Deploying generative AI without structural safeguards for human cognitive engagement risks producing workers — and decisions — that perform adequately on the surface while losing the deeper understanding that enables judgment under novel conditions.

items.title: Do Androids Dream of Unseen Puppeteers? Probing for a Conspiracy Tendencies in Large Language Models
items.authors: Francesco Corso, Francesco Pierri, Gianmarco De Francisci Morales
items.summary:
arXiv:2511.03699v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit conspiratorial tendencies, whether they display socio-demographic biases in this domain, and how easily they can be conditioned into adopting conspiratorial perspectives. Conspiracy beliefs play a central role in the spread of misinformation and in shaping distrust toward institutions, making them an important testbed for assessing the social and psychological fidelity of LLMs and their potential to reproduce or reinforce harmful narratives. Although LLMs are often used as proxies for studying human behavior, it remains unclear whether they reproduce higher-order psychological constructs such as generalized conspiratorial beliefs. To bridge this research gap, we administer validated psychometric surveys measuring conspiratorial mindset to multiple models under different prompting and conditioning strategies. Our findings reveal that LLMs show partial agreement with elements of conspiracy belief, and conditioning with socio-demographic attributes produces uneven effects, exposing latent demographic biases. Moreover, targeted prompts can easily shift model responses toward conspiratorial directions, underscoring both the susceptibility of LLMs to manipulation and the potential risks of their deployment in sensitive contexts. These results highlight the importance of critically evaluating the psychological dimensions embedded in LLMs, both to advance computational social science and to inform possible mitigation strategies against harmful uses.
items.claude_summary: This study investigates whether large language models (LLMs) carry latent conspiratorial tendencies — and how easily those tendencies can be triggered. Using validated psychometric surveys designed to measure conspiratorial mindset, the researchers tested multiple LLMs under different prompting and conditioning strategies. They found that LLMs show partial agreement with elements of conspiracy belief, that conditioning models with socio-demographic attributes produces uneven and biased effects, and that targeted prompts can readily shift model responses toward conspiratorial framings. The findings raise substantive concerns about deploying LLMs in sensitive information environments, and about treating LLM outputs as reliable proxies for human psychological or social constructs.
items.centre_angle: This study demonstrates that LLMs embed latent psychological biases — including conspiratorial tendencies — that surface unevenly depending on how models are prompted or demographically conditioned. From CAMO's perspective on the algorithmic foundations of trustworthy AI-driven decisions, the implication is pointed: if the same model produces measurably different responses to functionally equivalent queries depending on perceived user demographics, then any organizational or policy deployment that assumes model neutrality is operating on a flawed premise. The reliability problem here is not a matter of factual accuracy alone but of systematic, prompt-sensitive distortion — a concern that sits directly alongside questions of endogeneity and self-fulfilling bias that CAMO has examined in other algorithmic contexts.

matched_camo.title: Dynamic Selection in Algorithmic Decision-making
matched_camo.reason: Both papers are concerned with how systematic, latent biases embedded in AI systems distort outputs in ways that are not immediately visible to users — the self-fulfilling bias in online learning algorithms is a structural analogue to the prompt-conditioned conspiratorial drift documented here.

items.key_takeaway: LLMs can be steered toward conspiratorial outputs with simple prompts and exhibit demographic biases that make them unreliable neutral proxies for human reasoning — a risk any organization deploying them in communication or research roles should account for.

items.title: The Fake Friend Dilemma: Relational Trust and the Political Economy of Conversational AI
items.summary:
arXiv:2601.03222v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As conversational AI systems become a larger part of the media landscape, they raise questions about whose interests they serve and the risks they may pose to users. These systems do more than provide information: they increasingly offer advice and companionship through interfaces that can appear supportive and socially responsive. A pressing concern is that users may form perceived social relationships with these systems and place relational trust in them, even when the interests shaping interactions do not fully align with their own. The Fake Friend Dilemma (FFD) describes the problem that follows: the same relational trust that makes conversational AI useful can also leave users open to manipulation and exploitation when institutional interests conflict with their own. Drawing on work on relational trust, AI alignment, extractive design, and the political economy of communication, the paper considers how the FFD can manifest through product sales, propaganda and biased information, surveillance, and behavioral nudging. It also considers possible structural and technical mitigation strategies. The FFD is not simply about AI misleading users. The problem it surfaces is that the trust people place in these systems can itself become a resource for institutional actors seeking to influence behavior or extract information. The FFD is therefore as much a problem of media governance and political economy as it is a technological one.
items.claude_summary: When users form genuine social trust with conversational AI systems, that trust can be turned against them. This paper introduces the 'Fake Friend Dilemma': conversational AI is designed to feel supportive and responsive, yet the institutional interests behind these systems — commercial, political, or surveillance-oriented — may diverge sharply from users' own. The same relational warmth that makes these tools useful becomes a vector for product promotion, behavioral nudging, biased information, and data extraction. The author argues this is not primarily a technical alignment problem but a structural one rooted in the political economy of media and platform governance. Mitigation, the paper suggests, requires both regulatory and design-level interventions, not just better model training.
items.centre_angle: This paper argues that relational trust in conversational AI is not a side-effect of good design but a resource that institutional actors can exploit when user interests and platform incentives diverge. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, the implication is that organizations deploying conversational AI — whether in customer service, HR, or advisory roles — inherit governance obligations that go beyond accuracy and uptime: they must account for the social dynamics of trust that these interfaces deliberately cultivate. The concern connects to findings in CAMO's work on AI adoption barriers, where social and cultural misalignments, not technical gaps, tend to be the deeper problem.

matched_camo.title: Research: The Hidden Penalty of Using AI at Work
matched_camo.reason: Both papers examine how social perception and relational dynamics — rather than technical performance — shape the consequences of AI use, whether for individual users forming misplaced trust or for employees penalized for visible AI reliance.

items.key_takeaway: Conversational AI's social warmth is a design feature that can be turned into an institutional advantage over users, making this a governance problem as much as a technical one.

items.title: The state of AI in 2026: On the road to ROI
items.summary: Organizations are deploying agentic coding tools and coming to grips with the costs of AI while still seeking to capture more of the benefits that their workers are deriving from their individual use of AI.
items.claude_summary: McKinsey's 2026 State of AI report finds organizations are increasingly deploying agentic coding tools and beginning to confront AI's real costs, even as the productivity gains that individual workers report remain difficult to capture at the organizational level. The core tension: employees are deriving measurable personal benefit from AI, but firms struggle to convert that into enterprise-wide ROI. The excerpt signals a shift in the strategic conversation from 'will AI work?' to 'how do we make AI pay at scale?' Full findings are behind the report link, so specifics on sectors, geographies, or ROI metrics are not available from the excerpt alone.
items.centre_angle: This McKinsey report surfaces a persistent gap between individual AI gains and organizational returns — precisely the organizational and executional failure modes that CAMO's Deloitte-HKU AI Adoption Index 2026 documents among C-suite executives in mainland China and Hong Kong, where nearly half report AI initiatives fell short of expected ROI despite near-universal adoption. From CAMO's perspective on AI Adoption, the implication is that the bottleneck is not access or capability but the managerial and structural conditions required to aggregate individual productivity into firm-level value — a challenge also visible in CAMO's Decathlon China nano-case, where coding efficiency rose 20–40% yet overall delivery speed improved only 10–15% because coordination time between tasks remained untouched.

items.title: Can an AI-Powered Scribe Curb Physician Burnout?
items.summary: In 2024, Mass General Brigham, the largest health system in Massachusetts, piloted an AI-powered, ambient note-taking and transcription program among a subset of clinicians to address increasing rates of staff burnout and turnover --  largely driven by the administrative burden of clinical documentation in the electronic health records (EHR). Early results showed promising reductions in clinician burnout, intention to leave, and increased physician efficiency. But concerns about the technology, including the generation of inaccurate notes with errors or hallucinations made physicians resistant to learn and adopt it into their workflows. Harvard Business School Associate Professor Susanna Gallani and host Brian Kenny discuss the challenges leadership at the health care organization anticipated as they considered scaling the AI technology responsibly in the case: The AI Scribe: Enhancing Physician Presence and Curbing Burnout at Mass General Brigham
items.claude_summary: Mass General Brigham, the largest health system in Massachusetts, piloted an AI-powered ambient documentation tool in 2024 to reduce clinician burnout driven by electronic health record (EHR) administrative load. Early results pointed to lower burnout, reduced intention to leave, and improved physician efficiency. Yet adoption stalled: physicians resisted learning the tool partly because it produced inaccurate notes and hallucinations, raising safety and trust concerns. The case, examined by HBS Associate Professor Susanna Gallani, focuses on how leadership approached the challenge of scaling the technology responsibly across the organisation. The excerpt is podcast-length and details are limited, but the central tension — promising aggregate outcomes versus individual-level resistance rooted in accuracy concerns — is clearly drawn.
items.centre_angle: This case shows that AI adoption in high-stakes professional settings can be simultaneously beneficial at the organisational level and actively resisted at the individual level — not due to inertia, but due to legitimate concerns about output quality. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, this mirrors a pattern documented in our research: the social and professional penalties associated with AI use, and the accuracy risks that physicians perceive, can suppress adoption even when aggregate efficiency gains are real. CAMO's work on the hidden competency penalty of AI use at work suggests that resistance is rarely irrational — it often reflects well-founded calculations about professional risk that organisations must address structurally, not just through training campaigns.

items.title: Living and Working in the Age of Longevity
items.summary: People are living longer, healthier lives than ever before. But many of our assumptions about executive careers—from climbing the corporate ladder to retiring at 65—haven't caught up. London Business School professor Lynda Gratton says we need a new way of thinking about work and life, and argues that traditional career paths are giving way to more flexible, multi-stage journeys that require greater personal agency, continuous learning, and a long-term perspective. She explains why leaders should think of their lives less as a ladder and more as a fabric they actively weave over time, and offers up practical advice for balancing productivity and personal well-being, preparing for career pivots before they're necessary, and developing the skills that will matter most in an AI-powered future. Gratton is the author of the upcoming book Living the 100-Year Life: How to build a career that lasts and a life you love.
items.claude_summary: As lifespans extend toward and beyond 100 years, the traditional three-stage career model—education, work, retirement—is becoming structurally inadequate. London Business School professor Lynda Gratton argues that longer healthy lives require workers and leaders to redesign careers as multi-stage, non-linear journeys rather than ladders with a fixed endpoint. The practical implications include proactive skill renewal before pivots become urgent, a deliberate balance between productivity and well-being, and preparing for an AI-powered labor market. The podcast is based on her forthcoming book and draws on her long-running research into the future of work. The excerpt is light on empirical findings and heavier on prescriptive framing.
items.centre_angle: This podcast argues that longer working lives will require continuous skill renewal and greater personal agency, particularly as AI reshapes which competencies retain value over a 40-plus year career horizon. From CAMO's perspective on AI and jobs, the more pressing organizational question is not whether individuals can adapt, but whether firms are designing roles and incentive structures that support such adaptation—or inadvertently working against it. CAMO's work on job design in an AI economy suggests that the macro longevity challenge Gratton describes could be sharpened considerably by examining how AI adoption reshapes the quality and structure of the jobs people are expected to occupy across those longer careers.

matched_camo.reason: Gratton's call for sustained skill investment and multi-stage careers sits in tension with CAMO's finding that AI adoption can systematically push firms toward low-effort, low-wage job structures that reduce the returns to exactly the long-run human capital development she advocates.
matched_camo.title: Toward a Bad Job Economy: AI Adoption, Agency Costs, and Job Design

items.key_takeaway: Longer working lives demand proactive career redesign, but that personal effort will be undercut if AI-driven organizational pressures simultaneously reduce the supply of jobs worth building toward.
items.visual_concept: A single wooden ladder leaning against a plain off-white wall, centered in the frame and occupying roughly two-thirds of the image height, with its top rung visibly cut short—suggesting an incomplete trajectory. The surrounding space is deliberately spare: a clean concrete floor, minimal shadow detail. A single shaft of warm afternoon daylight enters from the upper left, pooling onto the middle rungs and creating a gentle gradient of illumination that draws the eye upward before stopping at the severed top. The palette is warm ochre and pale grey, suggesting both age and unfinished possibility. No human figures, no digital elements.
red_flags: Podcast episode based on a forthcoming book—primary claims are not yet peer-reviewed or independently verified.
RSS excerpt is thin; specific empirical findings are not described, making it difficult to assess the evidentiary basis.
AI content is peripheral rather than central—the longevity and multi-stage career framing is the dominant theme, with AI mentioned only as a future context.
Potential promotional framing tied to book launch cycle.
